pos: n. (Melchior Hoffman, c. 1495–1543, apocalyptic Anabaptist preacher)
etymology: Hebrew Malki-or, king of light, through Latin Melchior; German Hoffmann, a farmer, a steward of a manor.
biblical_def: Melchior Hoffman was a Swabian furrier who became a lay preacher, moved from Lutheran to Anabaptist convictions, and carried an apocalyptic message through the Baltic ports and the Low Countries with great effect. He taught that the last days had come, that Strasbourg was the New Jerusalem, and that Christ would return in 1533; he presented himself at Strasbourg in that year expecting to be imprisoned briefly as the prophecy required, and remained in that prison for ten years until he died. He also taught that Christ's flesh was not taken from the virgin but brought from heaven through her, which denies the incarnation at the point where Scripture is most explicit. The dictionary records both the prediction and the Christology as errors, and names the rule that forbids the first: of that day and hour knoweth no man (Mat 24:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apocalyptic as containing or pertaining to revelation, and prediction as a foretelling, a prophecy.
webster_full: APOCALYP'TIC, a. Containing or pertaining to revelation; disclosing; of or belonging to the Apocalypse.
PREDIC'TION, n. A foretelling; a previous declaration of a future event; prophecy.
FUR'RIER, n. A dealer in furs; one who dresses furs and makes them into garments.
INCARNA'TION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man.
scriptures: But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
Act 1:7
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.
But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.
I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.
corruption_summary: He fixed a date for the return of Christ and spent his last ten years in a Strasbourg prison.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors are named here. The first is date-setting, which Scripture forbids in terms that leave no room at all, and which every generation repeats because a date is more exciting than a watch. The second is the celestial-flesh Christology, held by Hoffman and after him by much of the Dutch radical wing: that the Son did not take his humanity out of Mary's substance but passed through her. That empties the incarnation of the very thing it was for, since what is not assumed is not redeemed, and a Saviour who did not take our nature cannot have borne our penalty in it.

The principle to recover is the plain prohibition and the discipline it imposes. “But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only” (Mat 24:36). The risen Lord closed the question again on the mount of Olives: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7). And the LORD's complaint against the uncommissioned prophet is exactly Hoffman's case: “I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran” (Jer 23:21).

“I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran” (Jer 23:21) — a furrier turned prophet.

pos: n. (Jan Matthys, d. 1534, Haarlem baker and self-styled prophet of Munster)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, in Dutch Jan; Matthys, from Hebrew Mattithyahu, gift of the LORD.
biblical_def: Jan Matthys was a baker of Haarlem who took up Melchior Hoffman's message, declared himself the prophet Enoch, and in 1534 made the Westphalian city of Munster the headquarters of a kingdom he announced. Those who would not be rebaptized were driven out in the February snow; property was declared common; the books of the city, apart from the Bible, were burned; and the bishop's army closed the siege. Matthys rode out of the gate with a handful of men, expecting deliverance, and was killed and dismembered. He had ruled the city for about two months. The dictionary states what he was: an uncommissioned prophet whose claim was tested by the plain test God gave for such claims, and failed it (Deu 18:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fanatic as a person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects, and anarchy as want of government.
webster_full: FANAT'IC, n. A person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects; one who indulges wild and extravagant notions of religion.
AN'ARCHY, n. Want of government; a state of society when there is no law or supreme power, or when the laws are not efficient.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place, for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
PRES'UMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; adventuring without reasonable ground of success; irreverent with respect to sacred things.
scriptures: But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.

Then the LORD said unto me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name: I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, neither spake unto them: they prophesy unto you a false vision and divination, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Two months as prophet-king of Munster, and killed in a sortie he believed could not fail.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the whole episode as what it was: a false prophet establishing a tyranny in the name of Christ, and the end of it was the discrediting of believers' baptism across Europe for a century. That consequence matters to this dictionary, which holds credobaptism from Scripture. Munster was not the fruit of baptizing believers; it was the fruit of an uncommissioned prophet, armed revolution, and the abolition of every outward restraint, and the peaceable Anabaptists who repudiated it, Menno Simons among them, said so at the time.

The principle to recover is that God gave a test for prophetic claims and the test is lethal to the claimant, not to the hearer. “But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die” (Deu 18:20). The LORD's own verdict on such men is given in advance: “The prophets prophesy lies in my name: I sent them not” (Jer 14:14). And the sword Matthys took up answered him: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).

“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — killed in a sortie, February 1534.

pos: n. (Jan Beukelszoon, 1509–1536, tailor and self-crowned king of Munster)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; of Leiden, the Dutch city of his birth.
biblical_def: John of Leiden was a tailor and innkeeper of Leiden who took command of Munster when Jan Matthys was killed, dissolved the council, had himself proclaimed king of the New Jerusalem, and ruled the besieged city for sixteen months with a court, a throne, a coinage and an executioner. He instituted polygamy on the authority of the patriarchs and took sixteen wives, killing one of them himself in the street. When the city fell in June 1535 he was tortured publicly and executed, and his body was hung in an iron cage from the tower of St Lambert's church, where the cage remains. The dictionary records this in full because the appeal he made is still made, that the practice of the patriarchs licenses what Christ forbade (Mat 7:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines usurp as to seize and hold in possession by force or without right, and tyrant as a despotic ruler, a cruel master.
webster_full: USURP', v.t. To seize and hold in possession by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne.
TY'RANT, n. A despotic ruler; a monarch, or other ruler or master, who uses power to oppress his subjects.
POLYG'AMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time.
RAV'ENING, ppr. Preying with rapacity; devouring with voracious eagerness.
scriptures: Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Mat 19:5
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Mat 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: A tailor crowned king of the New Jerusalem, sixteen wives, and an iron cage on a church tower.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named at its root. John of Leiden argued from Abraham, Jacob and David that a plurality of wives is permitted to the people of God, and the argument is still heard wherever the patriarchal narratives are read as precept instead of as record. Scripture reports the polygamy of the patriarchs and reports its fruit as well, which is grief in every single case; and our Lord settles the question not from Genesis 29 but from Genesis 2, going behind every later practice to the creation ordinance of one man and one woman.

The principle to recover is that marriage was defined at the beginning and that Christ's appeal to the beginning is final. “For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5). The conclusion follows in the next verse without qualification: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6). And the warning about such teachers was given beforehand: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15).

“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6) — Christ goes behind Genesis 29 to Genesis 2.
“inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15) — sixteen months of a court and an executioner.

pos: n. (Bernhard Rothmann, c. 1495–1535, theologian of the Munster kingdom)
etymology: Germanic Bernhard, bold as a bear; German Rothmann, a red-haired man, or a councillor.
biblical_def: Bernhard Rothmann was the educated man at Munster and therefore the most culpable. A chaplain who had read the Reformers and preached evangelical doctrine in the city before the radicals came, he moved to Anabaptist convictions and then supplied the kingdom with its theology: tracts defending the community of goods, the restitution of all things, the sword in the hands of the saints, and finally polygamy. He died in the city's fall. The pattern he represents is a permanent danger and not a sixteenth-century curiosity: a trained man lending his learning to a movement whose course he can see and will not check, finding texts for each new step after the step has been taken. Paul names the source of such a movement precisely: of your own selves shall men arise (Act 20:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apology as a defence or excuse, and restitution as the act of restoring to a former state.
webster_full: APOL'OGY, n. A defense; an excuse; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
RESTITU'TION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been deprived.
CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a court, a ship, or a regiment.
PER'VERSE, a. Turned aside; distorted from the right; obstinate in the wrong.
scriptures: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: The trained man who found a text for every step after the step was taken.
corruption_paragraphs: The error named here is the misuse of learning to justify what is already decided, which is the oldest service a theologian can render to a tyranny. Rothmann did not begin as a fanatic. He had preached the gospel in Munster, and he followed the movement step by step, publishing a defence of each new measure as it arrived, until he was defending a polygamous monarchy under siege. Scripture puts such men inside the church, not outside it, which is what makes them dangerous.

The principle to recover is that teachers arise from within and are to be tried by the written word and, after due admonition, rejected. “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). Peter gives the same warning for the whole age of the church: “there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” (2Pe 2:1). And the remedy is stated without sentiment: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10).

“who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” (2Pe 2:1) — a tract for each new measure.
“A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10) — and he died in the city's fall.

pos: n. (Hans Hut, d. 1527, Anabaptist missionary of Franconia and Moravia)
etymology: German Hans, a short form of Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Hut, a hat, a hatter.
biblical_def: Hans Hut was a book pedlar of Franconia who became the most effective Anabaptist missionary in the German south and east, baptizing in Austria, Bavaria and Moravia and leaving congregations behind him wherever he went. He had been at Frankenhausen where Thomas Muntzer's peasant army was destroyed, and he carried out of it an apocalyptic expectation, teaching that the saints would be sealed and the judgment would fall in 1528. He was arrested at Augsburg, tortured, and died in his cell in a fire whose cause has never been settled; his body was burned by sentence afterwards. The dictionary names the error and refuses to minimize the cruelty. A man may hold a false calculation and still be murdered by a magistrate acting outside his commission (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and seal as to confirm, to ratify, to mark with a stamp.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent to preach the gospel in a foreign country or among a distant people.
SEAL, v.t. To confirm; to ratify; to establish; to mark with a stamp, as evidence of standard exactness or legal size.
PED'LER, n. One who travels about the country with small commodities, which he offers for sale.
MAR'TYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Act 1:7
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.
But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
Luk 12:4
And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do.
corruption_summary: The south German mission's best preacher, a date set for 1528, and a death in custody.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things are said and neither cancels the other. Hut's sealing of the elect against a dated judgment was error, of the same family as Hoffman's and Matthys's, and it drew men into an expectation that broke them when the year passed. The magistrates who tortured him were also acting beyond anything God gave the sword to do. The civil power is ordained to punish wrongdoing, not to extract confessions of faith, and the Reformed tradition took generations to learn that distinction and did not learn it in 1527.

The principle to recover is that the magistrate's authority is real and bounded. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The date-setting was already forbidden: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7). And the Lord's comfort to men in Hut's position is explicit: “Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do” (Luk 12:4).

Greek phobeo (G5399) — to fear, to be afraid of; Luke 12:4.

“It is not for you to know the times or the seasons” (Act 1:7) — a judgment dated to 1528.
“Be not afraid of them that kill the body” (Luk 12:4) — he died in an Augsburg cell.

pos: n. (Ludwig Haetzer, c. 1500–1529, Zurich radical and translator of the Hebrew prophets)
etymology: German Ludwig, famous warrior; Haetzer, from a Swabian family name.
biblical_def: Ludwig Haetzer was one of the first of Zwingli's circle at Zurich to break with him, and he did real work before he came to grief. With Hans Denck he produced in 1527 the first German translation of the Hebrew prophets made from the Hebrew, a version so good that Luther's own translators drew on it and it went through many printings. He also wrote the earliest Reformed tract against images. By the end of his short life he had moved to a denial of the Trinity and of Christ's deity, and he was executed at Constance in 1529 on a charge of adultery. The dictionary states all of it. A man may serve the text of Scripture ably and deny the Lord whom the text proclaims, and the first does not cover the second (Joh 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heterodox as contrary to the received doctrine, and version as a translation.
webster_full: HET'ERODOX, a. Contrary to the faith and doctrine established in the true church; contrary to any received doctrine.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
IM'AGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue.
APOS'TASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: He gave Germany the prophets from the Hebrew and ended by denying the deity of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named and so is the gift. Haetzer's prophets were a genuine service to the German Bible, and the anti-Trinitarian position he reached is a denial of the faith, not a variant within it. The two sit together in one short life, which is an unwelcome fact about the usefulness of unconverted or apostatizing scholarship, and the dictionary does not resolve it by pretending either half away.

The principle to recover is that the deity of the Son is on the page and is the test. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). Thomas is answered, not corrected: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28). John closes his letter with the identification spelt out: “This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20). And the standard that tries a translator as surely as a preacher: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

“This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20) — executed at Constance in 1529.

pos: n. (Sebastian Franck, c. 1499–1543, German spiritualist, chronicler and radical)
etymology: Greek Sebastianos, from Sebaste, venerable; German Franck, a Frank, a free man.
biblical_def: Sebastian Franck began as a Catholic priest, became a Lutheran preacher, and then left every church there was. He concluded that the visible church had died with the apostles, that no outward ministry, sacrament or confession had any authority, and that God speaks directly to the individual spirit by an inward word of which Scripture is only the outward sign. He made his living by printing, soap-boiling and writing, produced a vast chronicle of world history notable for treating heretics sympathetically, and was expelled from one city after another. The dictionary names this as the root error of all later spiritualism, and the answer is the one Peter gives: the Scripture is not any man's private property to interpret by his own light (2Pe 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spiritualize as to refine intellectually, to give a spiritual meaning to, and individual as single, one, pertaining to one only.
webster_full: SPIR'ITUALIZE, v.t. To refine intellectually or morally; to give a spiritual meaning to; to convert to a spiritual sense.
INDIVID'UAL, a. Single; one; pertaining to one only; not divided.
CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
EN'THUSIASM, n. A belief or conceit of private revelation; the vain confidence or opinion of a person that he has special divine communications.
corruption_summary: He concluded the visible church died with the apostles, and that God speaks only within.
scriptures: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named exactly: the inward word set above or in place of the written word. Once that move is made, nothing can correct the individual, since every correction comes from outside and he has already ruled outside authority inadmissible. Franck is the fountainhead of a stream that runs through the Quakers' inner light, through nineteenth-century liberal religious consciousness, and into the modern person who says the Spirit has told him something the Scripture forbids. The claim cannot be argued with, which is its attraction and its refutation.

The principle to recover is that the written word is public, external and not private property, and that the church is a visible assembly with officers. “Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20). The assembling is commanded and the neglect of it named: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). And the flock has overseers the Holy Ghost appointed: “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28).

“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — a man who left every church there was.
“to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28) — and the flock still has overseers.

pos: n. (David Joris, 1501–1556, Dutch spiritualist Anabaptist prophet)
etymology: Hebrew David, beloved; Dutch Joris, from Greek Georgios, a husbandman.
biblical_def: David Joris was a glass painter of Delft who became, after the fall of Munster, the most influential of the Dutch radical prophets. He rejected the sword and the kingdom of Munster, which was to his credit, and replaced them with something subtler: a claim to direct revelation that put his own visions above Scripture, and a teaching that the third David had come and a wholly inward kingdom was being established in which outward sin no longer touched the regenerate spirit. He moved to Basel in 1544 under the false name Johann van Brugge, lived there for twelve years as a respectable burgher, and was discovered after his death, when his body was exhumed and burned. The claim he made is the one Scripture tests and condemns (Jer 23:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revelation as the act of disclosing to others what was before unknown to them, and dissimulation as the hiding under a false appearance.
webster_full: REVELA'TION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them; that which is revealed, particularly by God to man.
DISSIMULA'TION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; a feigning.
VIS'ION, n. Something imaginary; the mere production of fancy; a supernatural appearance.
ALI'AS, n. A second writ; also, an assumed or other name.
scriptures: I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: A prophet of his own visions who lived twelve years in Basel under a false name.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors are named. The first is private revelation set above the written word, which makes the prophet uncorrectable. The second is the antinomian inference that regularly follows it: that for the truly spiritual, outward conduct has ceased to signify, so that the inward kingdom licenses what the law forbids. Joris did not teach the Munster sword, and the dictionary credits him with that; he taught something that dissolved the law instead, which does the same work more quietly.

The principle to recover is that prophetic claims are to be tried, not received, and the trying is done by the written word. “I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied” (Jer 23:21). The duty is laid on every believer: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jn 4:1). And the measure is external and fixed: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test, to try; Hebrew shalach (H7971), to send, to commission.

pos: n. (Lelio Francesco Maria Sozzini, 1525–1562, Italian jurist and anti-Trinitarian)
etymology: Latin Laelius, a Roman family name, through Italian Lelio; Sozzini, a Sienese family name.
biblical_def: Lelio Sozzini was a Sienese lawyer of a distinguished legal family who left Italy for the Reformation and then could not stop asking questions. He corresponded with Calvin, Bullinger and Melanchthon, pressing doubts about the Trinity, the resurrection body, original sin and the authority of the creeds, and he was repeatedly warned and repeatedly returned to the same objections. He died at thirty-seven leaving papers that his nephew Faustus read and systematized. The dictionary names the method as well as the conclusion. A man who treats the central articles of the faith as open questions to be reasoned out afresh from first principles has already decided something, and what he has decided is that the church has no deposit (1Ti 6:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Antitrinitarian as one who denies the Trinity, and skepticism as doubt, or a doubting of the truth of revelation.
webster_full: ANTITRINITA'RIAN, n. One who denies the Trinity, or the existence of three persons in the Godhead.
SKEP'TICISM, n. The doctrines or opinions of a skeptic; universal doubt; doubt of the truth of revelation.
JU'RIST, n. A man who professes the science of law; one versed in the study of law.
DEP'OSIT, n. That which is lodged in the hands of a person for safe keeping.
scriptures: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
corruption_summary: A lawyer who treated the Trinity as an open question, and a nephew who read his papers.
corruption_paragraphs: Antitrinitarianism is named by its own name and traced to its source. Lelio Sozzini raised the doubts; his nephew Faustus organized them into a system; the Polish Brethren embodied it; and English and American Unitarianism descend from it. The common thread is the elevation of a particular account of reason over the text, so that whatever cannot be fitted into a unitary conception of God is explained away however plainly it is written.

The principle to recover is that the faith was delivered once and is kept, not re-derived. “O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20). It was given once for all: “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). And the text these men could not accommodate is the plainest sentence in the New Testament: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1).

“oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20) — reason set over the text.
“the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — dead at thirty-seven, his papers kept.

pos: n. (Fausto Sozzini, 1539–1604, founder of the Socinian system)
etymology: Latin Faustus, fortunate, auspicious; Socinus, the Latinized form of Sozzini.
biblical_def: Faustus Socinus took his uncle Lelio's doubts and built a religion out of them. Settling in Poland in 1579, he gathered the scattered anti-Trinitarian congregations into the body known as the Polish Brethren, and the catechism published after his death at Rakow states the system: one God in one person; Christ a man, miraculously conceived and exalted, but not God; no original sin imputed; no satisfaction of divine justice, since forgiveness needs no payment; and the atonement reduced to an example and a confirmation of a doctrine. He also wrote the first sustained argument that a God who could simply forgive would be unjust to require a death. The dictionary answers the argument where the apostle puts it: the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Tit 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Socinianism as the doctrines of the Socinians, who deny the divinity of Christ, and satisfaction as that which satisfies, atonement, payment.
webster_full: SOCIN'IANISM, n. The doctrines or system of the Socinians, who deny the divinity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity.
SATISFAC'TION, n. That which satisfies; amends; atonement; payment; indemnification.
UNITA'RIAN, n. One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, and ascribes divinity to God the Father only.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
scriptures: Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
corruption_summary: He built a religion out of his uncle's doubts, and modern Unitarianism descends from it.
corruption_paragraphs: The system is named and rejected in every part. Socinus denied the Trinity, the eternal deity of the Son, the imputation of Adam's sin, and the substitutionary satisfaction; and the denials hang together, because a merely human Christ cannot bear infinite wrath and a God who requires no satisfaction has no need of a cross. His argument that free forgiveness and required payment are incompatible assumes what Scripture denies, namely that God's justice is an optional attribute he may set aside at will. The Reformed answer, given at length by Owen and Turretin against exactly this writer, is that God cannot deny himself.

The principle to recover is that the Saviour is God and the satisfaction is real. “Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). Thomas's confession stands unrebuked: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28). The Son is the very impress of the Father's being and purged sins by himself: “Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3). And John leaves no ambiguity: “This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20).

“the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3) — against a merely exalted man.
“This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20) — the Rakow catechism answered.
